meta.privacy: No real tenant names, initials, addresses, or other personal identifiers are stored in this repository. Only placeholder labels (Unit A, Unit B, Tenant A1, etc.) and the user-supplied dates and amounts are used; those case facts are flagged unverified.
meta.verification: Each 'verified' value was read line by line from the linked official government page on 2026-11-06. Any value that could not be confirmed from an official source is left blank in verified columns and appears on the Flagged for Review page.
meta.legal_status: Informational summary of official sources, not legal advice.

sources.title: Learn about rent increases in San Francisco
sources.quote: The allowed rent increase percentage in San Francisco is 1.6%. The percentage is effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
sources.notes: Also states the 12-month rule, base-rent-only rule, no rounding up, 30/90-day notice, notice contents, rent increase license, and prohibition on additional-occupant increases.

sources.title: Current Rates, including Rent Increase, Relocation, Sec. Deposit
sources.quote: Allowable Rent Increase: 1.6% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027; 1.4% for March 1, 2025 – February 28, 2026; 1.7% for March 1, 2024 – February 28, 2025.
sources.notes: Official citywide rate table.

sources.title: Annual Rent Increase for 3/1/26 - 2/28/27 Announced (Jan 14, 2026)
sources.quote: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
sources.notes: Official announcement.

sources.title: Form 571 — Allowable Annual Increases 26-27 (PDF)
sources.notes: Official historical AGA rate table used for illustrative banking arithmetic only.

sources.title: Banked rent increases
sources.quote: A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase. If less than 24 months pass, the skipped increase is lost and cannot be imposed at a later date.
sources.notes: Also states banked increases do not expire during a tenancy, are not capped, and do not carry over to a new tenant; notice must state which part is banked.

sources.title: Annual rent increase for multiple years
sources.quote: In these situations, landlords may increase rent by adding up the allowable increases during that time period. Increases cannot be compounded. Landlords are not required to file a petition with the City to impose these types of rent increases.
sources.notes: Also states 30-day written notice (35 days if mailed) and base-rent-only calculation.

sources.title: Learn about San Francisco rental laws
sources.quote: Many residential units built on or before June 13, 1979 have both rent control and eviction protection. If your unit was built before June 14, 1979, and is not used as a single family dwelling, it may have both: Rent control; Eviction protection.
sources.notes: Directs users to the Property Information Map to check the building date. Lists partial and total exemptions.

sources.title: The Rent Ordinance (SF Administrative Code Chapter 37)
sources.quote: The Residential Rent Stabilization and Arbitration Ordinance. The Rent Board's version of the Rent Ordinance is not the official record of the laws or regulations of the City and County of San Francisco.
sources.notes: Links to the official publisher (American Legal) and to each section.

sources.title: SF Administrative Code §37.3 — Rent Limitations
sources.quote: A landlord who has reported the required information about their rental unit to the Rent Board as set forth in Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant's base rent by more than 60% of said published increase. In no event, however, shall the allowable annual increase be greater than 7%.
sources.notes: Also contains §37.3(a)(2) banking, §37.3(a)(8) additional-increase petition, §37.3(a)(11) additional occupants, §37.3(b) notice contents, and §37.3(b)(5) null-and-void rule.

sources.title: SF Administrative Code §37.10C — Use and Sale of Algorithmic Devices Prohibited
sources.quote: It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device described in subdivision (a) when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in San Francisco.
sources.notes: Applies to any landlord; tenant and nonprofit enforcement; up to $1,000 per violation.

sources.title: SF Administrative Code §37.10B — Tenant Harassment
sources.quote: No landlord ... shall do any of the following in bad faith: ... Influence or attempt to influence a tenant to vacate a rental housing unit through fraud, intimidation or coercion ... Violate any law which prohibits discrimination.
sources.notes: Civil, criminal, and Rent Board remedies; attorney fees for prevailing plaintiffs.

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations, Part IV (§§4.10–4.12)
sources.quote: Section 4.10 Notice ... Those landlords not seeking a rental increase which exceeds the limitations set forth in Section 37.3 of the Rent Ordinance shall inform the tenant in writing on or before the date the notice is given of [the portions of the increase]. Nothing in this section ... shall be interpreted as requiring any landlord to pass through any utility increase or to raise any tenant's rent.
sources.notes: Nonconforming notice can render the increase null and void.

sources.title: The Rent Board Housing Inventory / rent increase license
sources.quote: A landlord must have a current rent increase license on file with the Rent Board before any annual or banked rent increase can go into effect. ... The information entered in the housing inventory submission is public.
sources.notes: Annual deadline March 1; reporting applies to condominiums and buildings with fewer than 10 units since March 1, 2023.

sources.title: Landlord Petitions and Passthroughs
sources.quote: There are six types of rent increases that require the filing of a landlord petition. ... All petitions must be submitted on the forms provided by the Rent Board and must include supporting documentation.
sources.notes: Lists capital improvement, O&M, comparable units, Proposition I, utility, and §1.21 petitions.

sources.title: Operating and Maintenance Expense Petitions
sources.quote: When the annual allowable increase does not completely cover the landlord's yearly increase in operating and maintenance expenses for a property, a landlord may petition for an additional base rent increase of up to 7%.
sources.notes: Requires two consecutive comparison years; petition must be filed before serving the notice; notice before petition is void.

sources.title: Apply to raise rents for capital improvement costs
sources.quote: You must file a Capital Improvement Petition with the Rent Board before increasing the tenants' rent. ... Capital Improvement Petitions must be filed within five years of the completion of the capital improvement work.
sources.notes: Separate forms for 1–5 unit and 6+ unit buildings.

sources.title: Tenant Financial Hardship Applications
sources.quote: For all other types of rent increases or passthroughs, including annual and banked rent increases or rent increases authorized by the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, financial hardship relief is not available.
sources.notes: Hardship relief is limited to capital improvement, bond, utility, and O&M passthroughs.

sources.title: Report an unlawful rent increase or request a review of your rent history
sources.quote: There is no charge for filing the petition. There is no time limit for filing a petition. ... Usually within a few months after the petition is filed, it will be scheduled for an arbitration hearing before a Rent Board Administrative Law Judge.
sources.notes: Tenant may contest an increase; hearing is designed so no one needs an attorney, but a lawyer or representative is allowed.

sources.title: Petition for a Determination Pursuant to Section 6.14 and/or Costa-Hawkins
sources.quote: San Francisco's Rent Ordinance does not regulate the initial rent for a new tenancy, so landlords are permitted to set rents for new tenancies at market rate. ... Section 6.14 and Costa-Hawkins can be very complicated. For that reason, landlords and tenants are strongly encouraged to seek legal advice.
sources.notes: Describes 6.14 notice and Costa-Hawkins subtenant rules; either party may petition the Rent Board.

sources.title: Rent Increases Under Section 6.14 And Costa-Hawkins
sources.quote: In addition, a co-tenant, as opposed to a subtenant, is not subject to such a rent increase, regardless of when the co-tenant moved in. ... Since these provisions can be complicated, landlords and tenants should obtain legal advice.
sources.notes: A 6.14 notice must be served within a reasonable time (generally 60 days) after the landlord learns of the occupancy.

sources.title: Roommates and subletting
sources.quote: Landlords in San Francisco cannot charge more rent simply because a new roommate (or several) has moved into a unit. This is illegal, no matter what the lease itself says.
sources.notes: Also covers master-tenant proportional share rules.

sources.title: Rent Board Referral Listing
sources.quote: The Rent Board cannot refer you to individual attorneys, but staff will be glad to direct you to appropriate resources for advice and assistance. ... Please note that you do not need a lawyer to file a petition at the Rent Board.
sources.notes: Official City listing of tenant/landlord/community resources, including free legal clinics, tenant counseling, and landlord associations.

sources.title: Speak with a Rent Board counselor
sources.quote: Cost: Free. ... We provide counseling on subjects related to the Rent Ordinance. We cannot give legal advice. We will let you know when your question is one that should be answered by a lawyer.
sources.notes: Phone 415-252-4600; multilingual support.

sources.title: Form 1007 — Notice to Tenant Required by Rent Ordinance §37.9(c) (PDF)
sources.quote: Effective March 19, 2016, a copy of this Notice to Tenant must be attached to every notice to terminate tenancy. ... You are eligible for free assistance through the Tenant Right to Counsel Program.
sources.notes: This notice attaches to termination notices, NOT to rent-increase notices — a common point of confusion.

sources.agency: San Francisco Board of Supervisors / MOHCD
sources.title: Resolution File No. 231201 (Tenant Right to Counsel grant, adopted Jan 9, 2024)
sources.quote: San Francisco voters passed the No Eviction Without Representation Act of 2018 (Proposition F) on June 5, 2018 establishing a policy that tenants facing eviction shall have a right to legal representation in eviction proceedings.
sources.notes: Right to Counsel is officially described as covering eviction proceedings.

sources.title: Update to Algorithmic Devices Law (Oct 6, 2025)
sources.quote: Currently, under Rent Ordinance Section 37.10C, landlords are currently prohibited from using algorithmic devices to set rents or occupancy levels for residential rental units in San Francisco. ... Starting October 6, 2025, tenants' rights organizations will also be able to file civil lawsuits.
sources.notes: Official news on expanded enforcement.

sources.title: The California Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482)
sources.quote: The maximum rent increase for units under AB 1482 from August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027 is 8.8% in San Francisco. This does NOT apply for units under the rent increase limitations of the San Francisco Rent Ordinance.
sources.notes: Also lists exemptions, just-cause rules, required notices, and damages.

sources.agency: California Department of Justice — Attorney General
sources.title: Limits on Rent Increases
sources.quote: San Francisco Area ... Increase starts between 8/1/25 and 7/31/26: 6.3%; Increase starts between 8/1/26 and 7/31/27: 8.8%. ... If the rent increase cap set by your city or county results in a lower increase than the Tenant Protection Act, then the local rule will apply.
sources.notes: Official statewide cap chart; local SF row also lists 1.6% for 3/1/26–2/28/27.

sources.title: California Civil Code §827
sources.quote: If the proposed rent increase for that tenant is 10 percent or less ... the notice shall be delivered at least 30 days before the effective date of the increase ... If the proposed rent increase for that tenant is greater than 10 percent ... the notice shall be delivered at least 90 days before the effective date.
sources.notes: Also specifies personal delivery or service by mail under Code of Civil Procedure §1013.

sources.title: California Civil Code §1947.12 (AB 1482 rent cap)
sources.quote: An owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower.
sources.notes: §1947.12(d)(3) exempts housing already subject to a more restrictive local rent cap; §1947.12(e) requires notice per §827; §1947.12(d)(5)(A) denies the single-family exemption to REITs, corporations, and LLCs with a corporate member.

sources.title: California Civil Code §1946.2 (just cause)
sources.quote: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
sources.notes: State just-cause protection; SF's local just-cause rules are more protective (S27).

sources.title: California Civil Code §1954.53 (Costa-Hawkins)
sources.quote: If the original occupant or occupants who took possession of the dwelling or unit pursuant to the rental agreement with the owner no longer permanently reside there, an owner may increase the rent by any amount allowed by this section to a lawful sublessee or assignee who did not reside at the dwelling or unit prior to January 1, 1996. This subdivision does not apply to partial changes in occupancy ... where one or more of the occupants ... remains an occupant in lawful possession.

sources.title: California Government Code §12955 (Fair Employment and Housing Act)
sources.quote: It shall be unlawful: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
sources.notes: State protected classes are broader than the federal list.

sources.title: AB 325 (2025) — Cartwright Act: violations (Chapter 338)
sources.quote: This bill would also make it unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce.
sources.notes: Approved by Governor October 6, 2025; adds Business and Professions Code §§16729 and 16756.1.

sources.title: Justice Department Sues RealPage for Algorithmic Pricing Scheme (Aug 23, 2024)
sources.quote: The complaint alleges that RealPage contracts with competing landlords who agree to share with RealPage nonpublic, competitively sensitive information about their apartment rental rates and other lease terms to train and run RealPage's algorithmic pricing software.
sources.notes: Allegations in a civil antitrust complaint, not a finding of liability. Co-plaintiffs include the California Attorney General.

sources.title: Justice Department Sues Six Large Landlords for Algorithmic Pricing Scheme (Jan 7, 2025)
sources.quote: The Justice Department ... filed an amended complaint today in its antitrust lawsuit against RealPage, to sue six of the nation's largest landlords for participating in algorithmic pricing schemes that harmed renters. ... Together, these landlords operate more than 1.3 million units in 43 states and the District of Columbia.
sources.notes: Allegations, not findings. Describes centralized revenue-management practices among large landlords.

sources.agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
sources.title: Housing Discrimination Under the Fair Housing Act
sources.quote: The Fair Housing Act protects people from discrimination when they are renting or buying a home ... The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing because of: Race, Color, National Origin, Religion, Sex, Familial Status, Disability.
sources.notes: Housing discrimination is illegal in nearly all housing, including private housing.

sources.title: 24 CFR §100.500 — Discriminatory effect prohibited
sources.quote: Liability may be established under the Fair Housing Act based on a practice's discriminatory effect ... even if the practice was not motivated by a discriminatory intent. The practice may still be lawful if supported by a legally sufficient justification.
sources.notes: eCFR is authoritative but unofficial; current as of 11/04/2026 when checked.

sources.agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (archives)
sources.title: HUD Glossary of Terms to Affordable Housing
sources.quote: Rent Controls: Defined as state and local government actions that restrict rent increases or service fee charges to tenants.
sources.notes: HUD defines rent control as a state/local action; used only to frame the federal-law question. Archived 2006 glossary, not a current rate source.

sources.title: Rent Board — department home page
sources.quote: This year's allowed rent increase is 1.6%. For covered units, the allowable rent increase effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.
sources.notes: Links to forms, statistics, counseling, laws, and regulations.

sources.title: Rent Board Forms Center
sources.quote: This petition is for tenants who have received an unlawful rent increase and/or want the Rent Board to determine whether their current rent is a lawful amount. ... This petition is for tenants who have received a rent increase notice that is clearly unlawful on its face and has not yet gone into effect.
sources.notes: Official tenant forms 516C and 518.

sources.title: kanlerxz87-cyber/RentincreaseSF1
sources.quote: Repository initially contained only README.md (# RentincreaseSF1) at commit b2a2caf; GitHub Pages is configured to deploy from the main branch, root path.
sources.notes: Used only for repository-review facts, not for legal values.

facts.value: Units built on or before June 13, 1979 generally have rent control and eviction protection; units built before June 14, 1979 that are not used as a single-family dwelling may have both.
Units built after June 13, 1979; most single-family homes and condos (tenant moved in on/after Jan 1, 1996); substantially rehabilitated units; units regulated by another government agency.
Search the address on the City's Property Information Map; speak with a Rent Board counselor if the unit is hard to classify.
1.6% of base rent
1.4% of base rent
1.7% of base rent
60% of the published increase in CPI; in no event greater than 7%
1.6% announced January 14, 2026
Only once every 12 months; first increase 12 months after the lease began.
The effective date of an increase becomes the tenant's anniversary date; a later increase shifts the anniversary date.
Use the percentage in effect on the date the increase takes effect, not the date notice is served.
Base rent only (includes housing services such as parking/storage); excludes temporary passthroughs; cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar.
No limit on the initial rent first charged for an empty rent-controlled unit.
A landlord cannot charge additional rent simply because a new or additional roommate moved in; such an agreement is void.
A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase; otherwise it is lost.
Banked increases do not expire during a tenancy, are not capped, and may be combined with a regular annual increase; they do not carry over to a new tenant.
If only part of the allowable increase is used, the rest is banked and may be imposed later after at least 12 months.
Add up the allowable increases for the period; increases cannot be compounded; no Rent Board petition is required for these types of increases.
§37.3(a)(2) permits accumulating an annual increase or any portion thereof for subsequent anniversary dates.
30-day written notice; 90-day written notice if the increase (alone or combined with another increase in the same year) is more than 10%; add 5 days if mailed.
Dollar amount of the increase, percentage amount, and the date the increase goes into effect.

§37.3(b) requires written disclosure of which portion is annual/banked, which reflects O&M/comparable/capital improvement costs, and which reflects passthroughs; a nonconforming increase is null and void.
The notice must state which part of the increase is banked.
Landlords not seeking an increase above §37.3 must inform the tenant in writing, on or before the notice date, of each portion of the increase; nonconforming notice can void the increase.
30 days for increases of 10% or less; 90 days for increases over 10%; written notice delivered personally or served by mail under CCP §1013.
§1947.12(e) requires the owner to give notice of any increase in accordance with Civil Code §827.
Form 1007 must be attached to every notice to terminate tenancy; it is not a rent-increase notice.
A landlord must have a current rent increase license on file before any annual or banked increase can go into effect; the notice is unenforceable without it.
All residential owners must report; annual deadline March 1; reporting began March 1, 2023 for condominiums and buildings with fewer than 10 units.
Information entered in the Housing Inventory submission is public; owner/agent business contact information and unit characteristics are reported.
Six types require a landlord petition before serving the tenant with a notice of increase; all petitions require Rent Board forms and supporting documentation.
When the annual increase does not cover increased O&M expenses, a landlord may petition for an additional base rent increase of up to 7%; two comparison years are required.
A Capital Improvement Petition must be filed before increasing rent, after work is entirely completed, and within five years of completion.
§37.3(a)(8): a landlord seeking any rent increase exceeding those permitted must petition for a rental arbitration hearing under §37.8.
Financial hardship relief is NOT available for annual or banked rent increases (only for specified passthroughs and O&M increases).
A tenant may file an unlawful-rent-increase / rent-history petition at no charge with no time limit; an Administrative Law Judge holds an arbitration hearing.
Form 518 is for a pending rent increase that is clearly unlawful on its face and has not yet gone into effect.
Free counseling on Rent Ordinance topics; counselors cannot give legal advice and will say when a lawyer is needed.
Official City referral listing includes tenant counseling organizations, free limited-advice legal clinics, and landlord associations; no lawyer is needed to file a Rent Board petition.
The No Eviction Without Representation Act of 2018 (Proposition F) establishes a right to legal representation for tenants facing eviction.
8.8% (5% + 3.8% CPI) for increases effective August 1, 2026 – July 31, 2027, for units subject to AB 1482.
5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower; no more than two increases in a 12-month period.
Units already subject to the San Francisco Rent Ordinance's rent-increase limits are not subject to the AB 1482 cap; if the local cap is lower, the local rule applies.
San Francisco Area cap was 6.3% for increases starting August 1, 2025 – July 31, 2026.
After 12 months of continuous lawful occupancy, a tenancy cannot be terminated without just cause stated in the written notice.
§1954.53(d)(3): the unlimited-increase provision does not apply to partial changes in occupancy where one or more original occupants remains in lawful possession.
The single-family/condo exemption is unavailable if the owner is a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with at least one corporate member.

FEHA prohibits housing discrimination/harassment based on race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information.
Chapter 338 makes it unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy to restrain trade.
Prohibits housing discrimination because of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability; applies to nearly all housing including private housing.
24 CFR §100.500: liability may be based on a practice's discriminatory effect even without discriminatory intent, unless supported by a legally sufficient justification.
HUD's official glossary defines rent controls as state and local government actions that restrict rent increases or service fee charges to tenants.
DOJ alleged competing landlords shared nonpublic competitively sensitive rental data to train algorithmic pricing software that recommends rents.
DOJ sued six large landlords alleged to have set rents using competitors' sensitive information through common pricing algorithms; together they operate more than 1.3 million units.
§37.10C prohibits any SF landlord from using algorithmic devices (revenue-management software using non-public competitor data) to set rents or occupancy levels.
From October 6, 2025, tenants' rights organizations may also file civil lawsuits to enforce the algorithmic-device prohibition.
The Housing Inventory and rent-increase license requirements apply to all residential owners, including condominiums and buildings with 1–9 residential units.
The City's official referral listing names landlord membership organizations, including Small Property Owners of San Francisco and the San Francisco Apartment Association.

§37.10B prohibits bad-faith conduct including coercion to vacate through a rent increase substantially above market and violating anti-discrimination laws; prevailing plaintiffs may recover attorney fees.
Rent Board Rules §4.11(e): nothing in the rules requires any landlord to raise any tenant's rent.

flags.title: Building coverage not officially verified
flags.detail: The user says the building was built in 1940 and is rent controlled. Official SF.gov guidance says coverage depends on the certificate-of-occupancy date and several exemptions; the specific property was not checked against official records. No coverage value is asserted as verified.
flags.action: Check the address on the City's Property Information Map and confirm with a Rent Board counselor / SF tenant lawyer.

flags.title: Unit A occupancy change: 6.14 / Costa-Hawkins / additional-occupant issue
flags.detail: The user describes a continuing tenancy with a changed tenant list and an unchanged rent. Official sources say an unlimited market-rate increase is available only in specific situations (all original occupants gone, proper 6.14 notice, lawful sublessee), that a co-tenant is not subject to a Costa-Hawkins increase, and that §1954.53(d)(3) does not apply where an original occupant remains. The City strongly encourages legal advice. The correct characterization is not determinable from the supplied facts.
flags.action: Have an SF tenant lawyer review the lease, occupancy timeline, and any 6.14 notices before any increase beyond the annual allowable amount.

flags.title: Unit A anniversary / banking ambiguity
flags.detail: Lease start February 1, 2025 and continuing tenancy April 1, 2026 are both user-supplied. SF.gov examples show that changing the anniversary date can cause a skipped increase to be permanently lost. No case-specific anniversary or banking entitlement is asserted as verified.
flags.action: Confirm the lawful base rent, last increase date, and anniversary date with the Rent Board or a tenant lawyer.

flags.title: Unit B banked increases require a full rent history
flags.detail: The user-supplied lease start is June 1, 2019 with no increase history. SF.gov permits adding up banked increases under detailed conditions (24-month rule, no compounding, no carryover to a new tenant). No case-specific banked percentage or dollar amount is asserted as verified.
flags.action: Request a Rent Board determination of the lawful rent / full rent history before imposing any combined increase.

flags.title: All case dates and amounts are unverified user input
flags.detail: February 1, 2025; April 1, 2026; June 1, 2019; $3,995; $3,150 are supplied by the user only. They are retained verbatim for review but left blank in every verified-value column, per the verification rule.
flags.action: Compare against the signed leases, rent receipts, and Rent Board records.

flags.title: Compliance prerequisites unknown
flags.detail: Current rent increase license, Housing Inventory reporting, prior notices, petitions, passthroughs, and exemption/subsidy status were not supplied. A license must be on file before an annual or banked increase can go into effect.
flags.action: Verify in the Rent Board Portal and document the results before serving any notice.

flags.title: Reasonable / normal is not a defined legal term
flags.detail: Official sources publish the allowed annual increase (1.6%) but do not define 'reasonable' or 'normal' as a separate legal standard. No case-specific 'reasonable' figure is asserted as verified.
flags.action: Treat the published AGA and the documented per-unit rent history as the objective benchmark.

flags.title: No official source supports 'raise both units to avoid discrimination lawsuits'
flags.detail: No official source was found stating that increasing both units is required or creates a safe harbor. Official fair-housing sources prohibit discriminatory terms and practices with discriminatory effects; SF law prohibits bad-faith harassment. A uniform documented policy is an analysis recommendation, not a verified legal rule.
flags.action: Ask an SF tenant lawyer to review the written, uniformly applied policy and both units' files.

flags.title: No official source explicitly says 'no reason is required' for the annual increase
flags.detail: Official sources say the annual increase is available to a licensed landlord and list six increases that require a petition with supporting documentation; they do not explicitly state that no reason is required. This negative inference is flagged rather than asserted as verified.
flags.action: Confirm the notice content and justification language with a tenant lawyer.

flags.title: No federal rent-increase cap for private unsubsidized housing was confirmed
flags.detail: HUD's official glossary defines rent controls as state and local government actions, and federal fair-housing law governs discrimination. No official federal source establishing a numeric cap on private rent increases was found, so the federal cap cell is left blank rather than filled with an inference.
flags.action: Confirm with counsel if any federal subsidy or program applies to the property.

flags.title: No official comparative data on corporate vs individual rent-increase practices
flags.detail: Official sources document enforcement actions against large landlords using shared pricing algorithms and rules that apply to all owners, but no official source was found quantifying or describing how individual small owners typically set increases. No practice value is asserted as verified.
flags.action: Do not rely on unverified industry-practice claims; rely on the official rules that apply to all owners.

flags.title: Form 1007 is a termination-notice attachment, not a rent-increase notice
flags.detail: The official Form 1007 states it must be attached to every notice to terminate tenancy. It is sometimes mistaken for a rent-increase notice. Rent-increase notice requirements come from §37.3(b), Rules §4.10, Civil Code §827, and SF.gov guidance.
flags.action: Use the correct notice; do not attach Form 1007 to a rent-increase notice unless counsel advises it.

flags.title: Right to Counsel is described for eviction proceedings
flags.detail: The City's official resolution describes Proposition F as a right to legal representation for tenants facing eviction. Free general tenant counseling and legal-clinic referrals are listed separately by the Rent Board. No official source was found guaranteeing free counsel for a rent-increase dispute.
flags.action: Use the Rent Board Referral Listing for free counseling / clinics; engage counsel for a compliance review.

flags.title: Secondary sources conflict on the 2026–27 percentage
flags.detail: Non-official web pages were found quoting both 1.7% and 1.6% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027. The official SF.gov rate table, news announcement, and Form 571 all state 1.6%; 1.7% belongs to the 2024–25 period.
flags.action: Use official SF.gov / Rent Board figures only; do not cite secondary calculators.

flags.title: Repository initially had no coordination board or site
flags.detail: At the starting commit b2a2caf the repository contained only README.md ('# RentincreaseSF1'). COORDINATION.md did not exist and was created by this session; no source data, site, or verification script existed to review line by line.
flags.action: Review the new files and the source register on the site.

flags.title: Parallel sessions claimed overlapping file scopes
flags.detail: Two other remote branches (arena/2347590f..., arena/da7cfb4c...) published COORDINATION.md claims; one claimed all site/data tasks and the other claimed docs/**, scripts/**, and workflows. This session therefore used a disjoint root-level scope (index.html, pages/**, assets/**, data/**, and root-level docs) and did not edit those files.
flags.action: Confirm no duplicate or conflicting site files were merged to main.

flags.title: No ZIP-code-specific official rate was found
flags.detail: The Rent Board publishes one citywide allowable increase; no official source was found setting a different rate for ZIP 94122 or the Outer Sunset. The citywide rate is used, and no ZIP-specific value is asserted.

flags.title: Market conditions are not an official standalone ground for an extra increase
flags.detail: Official SF sources list six petition-based grounds (capital improvement, O&M, comparable units, Proposition I, utility, §1.21). No official source was found allowing a general 'market rate' or 'inflation' justification above the AGA for an existing tenancy.
flags.action: Do not cite market conditions as a justification for an above-AGA increase without an approved petition.

scenarios.assumption: Illustrative only: continuing tenancy with at least one original occupant, unchanged lawful base rent, and an increase effective April 1, 2026 (user-supplied date).
scenarios.note: 1.6% is the official rate effective March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027. $3,995 is user-supplied and unverified; no case-specific result is asserted as verified. A 30-day notice applies because the increase is 10% or less.

scenarios.assumption: Illustrative only: apply only the current annual allowable increase to the user-supplied $3,150 base rent; no banked increases used.
scenarios.note: 1.6% is the official rate; $3,150 is user-supplied and unverified. 30-day notice applies.

scenarios.assumption: Illustrative only: arithmetic sum of the officially published annual rates for the seven anniversary dates from June 1, 2020 through June 1, 2026 (1.8% + 0.7% + 2.3% + 3.6% + 1.7% + 1.4% + 1.6% = 13.1%), applied without compounding to a user-supplied $3,150 base rent. This is NOT a determination of the lawful banked increase.
scenarios.note: Banking eligibility depends on the 24-month rule, the anniversary date, and the full rent history. A combined increase above 10% requires 90-day written notice under Civil Code §827 and SF.gov guidance. Consult the Rent Board / a tenant lawyer before relying on this figure.
